metadata.title: Employment and productivity in an ageing society: Japan in international perspective
metadata.venue: The Journal of the Economics of Ageing

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This paper does not conduct an original student-level large-scale assessment analysis (e.g., no PIAAC microdata model estimation with sampling weights). Instead, it synthesizes demographic and labour-market evidence for Japan and compares it with other OECD economies using externally sourced statistics and prior research. Because no ILSA microdata are analyzed, there is no need to apply student sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) for variance estimation. If future work uses PIAAC microdata for predictive modeling, analysts should apply the PIAAC sampling weights provided in the international database and use replicate weights (if available) to obtain correct standard errors under the complex survey design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the study is not an empirical ILSA microdata analysis predicting cognitive achievement scores (e.g., PIAAC literacy/numeracy PV-based outcomes). The paper is a narrative synthesis of demographic, employment, productivity, and technology adoption evidence, drawing on published statistics and prior studies rather than estimating PV-based models from ILSA microdata. Missing-data handling is therefore not part of the reported methodology because no analytic dataset with item-level missingness is constructed for ML estimation in this paper.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No ILSA microdata sample is constructed. The paper uses descriptive and comparative evidence for Japan and other OECD economies from external sources (e.g., UN World Population Prospects, OECD statistics, WHO, and cited research), rather than an assessment micro-dataset with an analytic subsample defined by item/task completion or PV availability.

data.outcome_summary: This article is not an empirical large-scale assessment (ILSA) machine-learning study. It provides an economic perspective on how population ageing affects labour supply, productivity, innovation, technology adoption (including AI/robotics), and public finances, with Japan as the focal case and comparisons to other OECD economies. The paper reports multiple descriptive statistics and decomposition-style results (e.g., GDP per capita growth decomposition, employment rates by age, dependency ratios, and spending shares) drawn from external datasets and prior literature rather than from a single ILSA microdata analysis. Because no student-level assessment dataset is modeled, there are no ML targets, no predictive performance metrics (e.g., RMSE/AUC), and no survey-weighted estimation procedure. Consequently, the methodological implications are about policy interpretation of demographic and productivity channels, not about model-based prediction or causal identification from ILSA data.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse because the manuscript is a narrative economic analysis and literature synthesis rather than an empirical ML paper using ILSA microdata. As a result, there is no assessment cycle/grade/domain, no analytic student sample, no plausible-values or missing-data handling protocol, and no ML algorithm training/evaluation reported. The absence of these fields reflects the study design (review/synthesis) rather than a reporting gap in an ML pipeline.
